paras: The attempted lynching of Albert Hayes took place at about one o'clock in the morning of June 7, 1881, when a body of masked men broke into the county jail at Cairo, Illinois, to take and hang Hayes, a young Black prisoner. The men broke through a door and two of three cell locks but dispersed after the jail's keeper confronted them and fire bells were rung, and Hayes was held for trial.

Hayes was charged with assaulting Mrs. Kobler, described by a Cairo wire as "an old German woman," above the city on the evening of June 3. According to the wire report, a Black man passing by rescued her. Sheriff Hodges, Marshal Myers and Officer John Tyler captured Hayes at his home at Twenty-ninth and Sycamore streets about eleven that night and lodged him in the county jail.

The Cairo Bulletin described Hayes as about nineteen and lately released from the state reform school, and the officers said he had confessed, though he denied part of the account. The same paper later noted that "numerous threats" against him had been heard in the following days.

The Bulletin put the mob at about forty masked men, while a Cairo dispatch to the Chicago Tribune said about thirty. Finding the outer doors open because of the heat, they entered the jail and held Mike and John Fitzgerald, sons of Richard Fitzgerald, at gunpoint as they slept in the hall. Mike was threatened with "instant death" unless he produced the keys, until John appeared with a shotgun and won his release, then ran across the street for his father.

Meanwhile the men broke open the door to the cell hallway with a crowbar and axe and destroyed two of the three locks on Hayes's cell. Richard Fitzgerald, unarmed, ordered them out and told them they would have to injure him and his sons before they could take the prisoner, and the fire bells he had ordered rung began to sound. The mob dispersed and threw the axe and crowbar over the courtyard fence.

That afternoon Hayes, "very much scared," was brought before Esquire Osborn, waived examination, and was held in $500 bond for the July term of the circuit court, with D. T. Linegar as his counsel. A rumor that twelve men from Kentucky had been brought in for a second attempt came to nothing by late that night. No arrests of mob members, and no outcome of Hayes's case, appear in the coverage.

The Cairo Bulletin covered the case most fully, headlining its account "Attempt at Lynching" and calling Hayes a "young rascal" and "youthful devil." Its editorial comment granted "ample cause for indignation" but held that taking him from the law was "also a crime," and it called the raid a "grotesque affair." In July the paper boasted that but for "Jailer Fitzerald and posse" Hayes would have been hanged within six hours of the crime.

Outside Cairo, the Wheeling Intelligencer printed the wire report of the arrest on June 6, and the Chicago Tribune ran a brief special headed "Discomfited Lynchers" on June 8. Both papers stated the charge against Hayes as fact, and no Black-press coverage is available for 1881.

The accounts differ on how the mob was stopped: the Bulletin credits Richard Fitzgerald's stand and the bells, while the Tribune says one of the jailer's sons fired a revolver. The accuser's name is spelled Kobler, Koehler and Kublor, and the July Bulletin names Officer Olmsted rather than Sheriff Hodges among the arresting officers.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Hayes
bases: A body of masked men broke into the Cairo county jail to take and hang Albert Hayes, a Black prisoner, but were driven off before reaching him (A3, A4, A8).
About thirty to forty masked men tried to take Hayes from jail to lynch him over an accused assault, but no one was killed (A3, A4, A8); this was an attempted lynching.
The local Cairo Bulletin and a separate Cairo special dispatch to the Chicago Tribune both describe the masked mob's failed attack on the jail (A3, A4, A8).

accounts.label: Cairo Bulletin local report
accounts.gist: About forty masked men entered the open jail, threatened the Fitzgerald sons, broke a door and two cell locks, and left after Richard Fitzgerald, unarmed, faced them and the fire bells rang.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune Cairo dispatch
accounts.gist: About thirty masked men tried to break the outer door to the cells with axes; the jailer and his two sons ordered them off, and a son's revolver shot quelled the mob.

accounts.label: Officers' account of the arrest
accounts.gist: Officers said Hayes confessed in their presence, though he denied dragging the woman by the hair.

framing.detail: The Cairo Bulletin headlined 'Attempt at Lynching', called Hayes a 'young rascal', 'young wretch' and 'youthful devil' and the crime 'heinous', but said taking him from the law was 'also a crime' and called the raid 'grotesque'.
The Chicago Tribune ran a short Cairo special headed 'Discomfited Lynchers', stating as fact that Hayes 'committed a rape'.
Six weeks later the Bulletin boasted that but for Jailer Fitzgerald 'the wretch would have been hung within six hours'.

conflicts.note: The local Bulletin account is more detailed; neither is clearly better.
